# Wants and plans {#wants-and-plans}

## The gap {#gap}

*I want to visit in March* and *I'm visiting in March* can sound like the same promise, so a wish said out loud is easily taken as a commitment you now owe someone. *I will* does not say how far a plan is worked out: whether you have backups, the steps, or only a direction. Ageben has separate words for a want and a plan, and the ending on each says how long the want lasts or how far the plan is worked out.

## The forms {#forms}
<!-- Agent summary: two sets of drop-ins. Want `thalol` / `thalom` / `thalor`: you wish the act would happen; says nothing about meaning to do it. Plan `thagol` / `thagom` / `thagor`: you mean to do it. Neither claims the act happens. Placement: where English puts an adverb or tag, usually the end of the clause; covers its clause. No ending clearly fits → middle one: `thalom` (length unsaid), `thagom` (how much is worked out unsaid). Omit both when only saying what happens (plain *I'm visiting in March*). -->

The drop-ins in this lesson come in two sets of three. A want word says that you wish an act would happen, and it says nothing about whether you mean to do it. A plan word says that you mean to do the act. Neither word claims that the act will happen.

| Drop-in | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `thalol` / `thalom` / `thalor` | want to: for a long time / for no stated length (the default) / right now, and it will pass |
| `thagol` / `thagom` / `thagor` | mean to: with backups ready / with the steps laid out (the default) / with only the direction |

Put the drop-in where English would put an adverb or a tag, usually at the end of the clause. Wherever it goes, it applies to the whole clause it sits in. When no ending clearly fits, use the middle one. `thalom` says you want to and leaves out how long, and `thagom` says you mean to without saying how much of the plan is worked out.

Leave both words out when you are only saying what happens. *I'm visiting in March* with nothing added says that the visit happens. *I'm visiting in March `thalom`* says that you want to visit, and it leaves open whether you will.

## What the ending says {#endings}
<!-- Agent summary: endings follow the settled-to-passing scale from *How sure are you?*: `-l` lasting, `-m` the default, `-r` right now; each word gives them its own meaning. Want = how long the wanting lasts: `thalol` keeps coming back, `thalom` unsaid, `thalor` will pass. Plan = how fully worked out: `thagol` backups ready (hurdles anticipated and prepared for), `thagom` steps laid out or detail unsaid, `thagor` direction only, details open. No plan level is better; a direction often suits a small or early plan; for a plan that matters, have an answer to what could go wrong before saying `thagol`. `thagom` on your own plan implies no backups yet. -->

The endings `-l`, `-m`, and `-r` are the three from *How sure are you?*, where they run from lasting to passing. Think of `-l` as *lasting*, `-m` as the default in the middle, and `-r` as *right now*. Each word gives the three endings its own meaning along that line.

### On a want {#on-a-want}

On a want word, the ending says how long the wanting lasts. For example, here is the same wish with two endings:

> I'm quitting my job `thalol`.  
> I'm quitting my job `thalor`.

With `thalol`, it is a want that keeps coming back, one you have had for a long time. With `thalor`, you feel like quitting right now, and the want will pass. The default, `thalom`, says you want to quit and leaves the length unsaid.

### On a plan {#on-a-plan}

On a plan word, the ending says how far the plan is worked out. Here is one plan with each ending:

> I'm asking for a raise `thagol`.  
> I'm asking for a raise `thagom`.  
> I'm asking for a raise `thagor`.

With `thagol`, you have backups ready: you have thought about what could go wrong, such as a no, and you know what you will do then. With `thagom`, the steps are laid out, such as when to ask and what figure to name. With `thagor`, you have the direction, and the details are still open.

No level is better than the others, so choose the one that matches the plan. A direction is often all a small or early plan needs. For a plan that matters, work out what could go wrong and have an answer ready before you say `thagol`.

You know how far your own plan is worked out, so `thagom` about your own plan implies that you have no backups yet. If you had them, you would say `thagol`.

## Examples {#examples}

> I'm taking a sabbatical `thalom`.  
> I'm going back to school `thalol`.  
> I'm calling in sick `thalor`.  
> I'm moving in the spring `thagol`.  
> We're redoing the kitchen `thagor`.

*I'm going back to school `thalol`* is a want you have had for years, and it does not say that you will go. *I'm calling in sick `thalor`* is a want that will pass, perhaps by lunchtime. *I'm moving in the spring `thagol`* says the plan already covers what you will do if the lease falls through, while *we're redoing the kitchen `thagor`* says that only the idea is settled.

## Telling them apart {#telling-apart}
<!-- Agent summary: near misses. Want vs plan: English *I'm going to* can introduce either; want word = a wish, no claim you mean to act; plan word = you mean to. Both together: want word first (`thalol` `thagom`). Plan vs forecast: a forecast (*I'm going to be late*) says what you expect to happen and takes no plan word; with `thagom` it becomes something you mean to do and no longer says it will happen. Whose: both words are always the speaker's, even when someone else does the act (*Sam takes the late shift `thalom`* = you want Sam to); someone else's own want or plan has no drop-in here, so it stays English. Wanting a thing: name the act that would get it (*I'm adopting a dog `thalom`*). -->

Four cases are easy to get wrong, and each is handled differently.

### A want or a plan {#want-or-plan}

English *I'm going to* can introduce a wish or something you mean to do, so the drop-in says which one you mean. *I'm going to learn Spanish `thalol`* says you have wanted to for a long time, and it does not say you mean to start. *I'm going to learn Spanish `thagom`* says you mean to, and that you have the steps laid out.

When you want something and also mean to do it, use both words, with the want word first. For example, *I'm going to learn Spanish `thalol` `thagom`* says that you have long wanted to and that you plan to.

### A plan or a forecast {#plan-or-forecast}

English *going to* also makes forecasts, which say what you expect to happen. *I'm going to be late* is usually a forecast, so it takes no plan word. With one, as in *I'm going to be late `thagom`*, the sentence says that you mean to arrive late, and it no longer claims that you will.

### Whose want or plan {#whose}

Both words always mean your own want or plan, even when someone else does the act. For example, *Sam takes the late shift `thalom`* says you want Sam to take it, and *Sam takes the late shift `thagom`* says you plan for Sam to take it. These drop-ins cannot say what Sam wants or plans, so for that, keep the sentence in English: *Sam wants the late shift*.

### Wanting a thing {#wanting-a-thing}

A want word goes on a sentence about an act. So for *I want a dog*, name the act that would get you the dog: *I'm adopting a dog `thalom`* says you want to adopt one.

## Practice {#practice}

Add the drop-in that fits the note.

**1.** *I'm switching teams.* (you mean to, and you've worked out what to do if it falls through)

::: details Show answer
I'm switching teams `thagol`.
:::

**2.** *I'm writing a novel.* (a wish that keeps coming back; you aren't saying you mean to)

::: details Show answer
I'm writing a novel `thalol`.
:::

**3.** *We're spending August in Lisbon.* (you have the direction; nothing is booked)

::: details Show answer
We're spending August in Lisbon `thagor`.
:::

**4.** *I'm trading my shift away.* (you mean to, and you have the steps)

::: details Show answer
I'm trading my shift away `thagom`.
:::

**5.** *I'm going to learn Spanish.* (a wish you've had for years; you aren't saying you mean to)

::: details Show answer
I'm going to learn Spanish `thalol`.
:::

**6.** *I'm going to learn Spanish.* (you mean to, and you've laid out the steps)

::: details Show answer
I'm going to learn Spanish `thagom`.
:::

**7.** *I'm skipping the party.* (you feel like it right now, and it will pass)

::: details Show answer
I'm skipping the party `thalor`.
:::

**8.** *I'm skipping the party.* (you want to; you aren't saying for how long)

::: details Show answer
I'm skipping the party `thalom`.
:::
